answer_text:
Decoder-bench memory experiment used for the comparison

* code family: `bb_code` distance 6, bivariate bicycle qLDPC
* noise: decoder-bench SI1000 circuit-level noise, `p = 0.0005`
* rounds = distance, Z-basis memory

* detectors = 252, observables = 12

Circuit-level noise attaches an error to every operation in the syndrome-extraction circuit — each gate, idle step, reset, and measurement — rather than depositing errors only on the data qubits between rounds. It is the realistic noise setting for QEC, and thresholds quoted “under circuit-level noise” are far more meaningful than code-capacity or phenomenological numbers. [^1]

SI1000 is a “superconducting-inspired” model calibrated to a 1000 ns cycle, with idle errors, weaker single-qubit gate error, and stronger measurement/reset error, reflecting real transmon device characteristics. These are the models implemented in Stim and used for most modern surface-code threshold estimates. [^1]

The FTPrimitiveBench description notes that SI1000 assigns operation-dependent error rates using a single base parameter p; for example, single-qubit gates are scaled as p/10, two-qubit gates as p, and measurement operations as 5p. [^3]

Results on the identical syndrome samples:

* `relay_bp` – IBM Relay-BP
  * logical error rate = 0.0
  * std error = 0.0
  * num_errors = 0 / 4000 shots
  * decode_seconds = 3.461
  * ok = true

* `mwpf` – hypergraph minimum-weight parity factor
  * logical error rate = 0.0
  * std error = 0.0
  * num_errors = 0 / 4000 shots
  * decode_seconds = 2.685
  * ok = true

Ranking by logical error rate

Both decoders observed zero logical failures in the 4 000-shot SI1000 memory run, so they are tied at an empirical logical error rate of 0.0 with no statistically distinguishable difference at this p and shot budget. The tool reports `best = "mwpf"` on the tie-breaker of decode time; MWPF is ~2.69 s vs Relay-BP ~3.46 s for the same 4 000 shots.

Like other qLDPC codes, BB codes are decoded with BP+OSD; the IBM demonstrations report pseudo-thresholds around ∼0.7% under circuit-level noise, in the surface-code ballpark but with an order-of-magnitude overhead saving. [^9]

The SI1000 model is the superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise model with operation-dependent error rates used for modern surface-code threshold estimates [^2]. Circuit-level noise attaches an error to every operation in the syndrome-extraction circuit and captures hook errors [^2]. Decoding is the classical inference problem of turning a syndrome $s = H E$ into a correction without incurring a logical error, with accuracy setting the threshold and speed setting the real-time latency budget [^1].

qLDPC codes keep checks sparse but encode $k = \Theta(n),\; d = \Theta(n)$ and are decoded with BP+OSD because checks are high-weight and non-graphlike [^3]. Standardized benchmarking efforts such as decoder-bench provide platforms for comparing decoder accuracy, speed and scalability [^4]. FTPrimitiveBench discussion notes SI1000 as a hardware-motivated noise model assigning operation-dependent error rates with a single base parameter $p$ [^5].

Circuit-level noise attaches an error to every operation in the syndrome-extraction circuit — each gate, idle step, reset, and measurement — rather than depositing errors only on the data qubits between rounds [^1]. Circuit-level noise attaches an error to every operation in the syndrome-extraction circuit — each gate, idle step, reset and measurement — rather than depositing errors only on the data qubits between rounds. Circuit-level noise context:

A circuit-level noise model attaches an error to every operation in the syndrome-extraction circuit — each gate, idle step, reset, and measurement — rather than depositing errors only on the data qubits between rounds. [^1]

* SD6 — a "standard depolarizing" model with six error locations, applying single- and two-qubit depolarizing channels of strength p after each operation, plus measurement/reset flips at rate p. [^1]
* SI1000 — a "superconducting-inspired" model calibrated to a 1000 ns cycle, with idle errors, weaker single-qubit gate error, and stronger measurement/reset error, reflecting real transmon device characteristics. [^1]

These are the models implemented in Stim and used for most modern surface-code threshold estimates. [^1]

decoder-bench is a framework for benchmarking decoders on relevant quantum error correction (QEC) code traces. It integrates with Stim … to generate traces (as check matrices, syndromes, and observables) for a variety of QEC codes and fault-tolerant subroutines. [^3]

The authors use decoder-bench to evaluate the accuracy and latency performance of multiple decoders across circuit-level simulations of color code memory experiments, bivariate-bicycle code memory experiments, surface code memory experiments, and surface code lattice surgery experiments. [^3]

SI1000 is also described as a superconducting-inspired noise model that assigns operation-dependent error rates using a single base parameter p; for example, single-qubit gates are scaled as p/10, two-qubit gates as p, and measurement operations as 5p. [^4]
